constructed/fixed over a long period and just using codes rather than
labels would defeat the purpose/simplicity of the reshape package.

disappear.

Thanks

Cheers
Peter

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I only recently discovered, inside the ggplot2 book, the great syntax with transform() to get ddply to add a new column with per-group computed values, akin to SQL windowing functions.  E.g.:

> x=movies[movies$year %in% c(2000,2005), c('title','year','rating')] d=rbind(x[x$year==2000,][1:2,], x[x$year==2005,][1:2,])
> d
               title year rating
6               $pent 2000    4.3
72            ...Lost 2000    6.2
79  ...al fin, el mar 2005    5.0
402    37 og et halvt 2005    5.6

> ddply(d, .(year), transform, mean_rating_by_year = mean(rating))
              title year rating mean_rating_by_year
1             $pent 2000    4.3                5.25
2           ...Lost 2000    6.2                5.25
3 ...al fin, el mar 2005    5.0                5.30
4    37 og et halvt 2005    5.6                5.30

But what I like most about it (and a similar technique of using subset()) is the use of extra named arguments that get evaluated in context of the data, without having to use the somewhat verbose syntax of a new closure and a data.frame() internal call.  So for the simpler case of by()-style / GROUP BY-style aggregation, instead of the usual

> ddply(d, .(year), function(x) data.frame(mean_rating = mean(x$year)))
  year mean_rating
1 2000        2000
2 2005        2005

I'd like to use the syntax

> ddply(d, .(year), newdf, mean_rating = mean(year))

... I wrote that newdf() myself to make the above work, like so:

newdf = function(.data, ...) {
  e = eval(substitute(list(...)), .data, parent.frame())
  data.frame(e)
}

... But, I suspect such a function might already exist, and in any case I'm new to R meta-ish programming and wrote that just by hacking up the transform() source.

Does anyone whether I'm re-inventing the wheel?

Thanks, Brendan

--

messages.subject_clean: Data altering bug in ddply with .drop=FALSE
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

The argument .drop=FALSE is not explicitly document for ddply, even
though it exists in the help. I figured it would work as for cast
i.e. .drop=FALSE would return all intersections of splitting
variables, including those with no data. It does that but the labels
for the split variables are wrong which means that the result values
get associated with the wrong combinations of factors:

library("plyr")

d = read.table(textConnection(
"x y foo value
1 1 bla 0.1719290
1 2 bla 0.6772318
1 2 bla 0.8376156
2 1 bla 0.5306457
1 1 bli 0.8027552
2 1 bli 0.8003605
2 1 bli 0.5801413
2 2 bli 0.4190968"
), header=T, sep=" ")

r1 = ddply(d, ~x+y+foo, function(x) sum(x$value))

r2 = ddply(d, ~x+y+foo, function(x) sum(x$value), .drop=FALSE)

r1
r2
r2[order(r2$x, r2$y, r2$foo),]

In r2 the values are in the same order as in r1, with the zeros added.
But the columns x, y and foo are in a different order. Ordering them
as in r1 reveals that the values associated with each combination are
not the correct ones.

This is a pretty serious bug since it returns a seemingly valid
data.frame (no warnings, correct dimensions) but with faulty data in
it. I guess that will tech me not to use undocumented features (plus
I'm kind of stubborn since this already happened to me with df=TRUE in
cast which was not documented and later disappeared...). But may I
suggest to remove the argument from the documentation while it is
being fixed?

Below is a patch and I also forked plyr on github (I am not sure what
is easiest, I've not yet used git for collaboration much).

Thanks in advance.

JiHO
